title: Performance and Reliability
description: Latency, throughput, caching, rate limiting, retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, queues, observability, and graceful degradation.

lessons.title: Latency and Throughput
lessons.summary: Latency is time per request; throughput is completed work per time period.
lessons.explanation: Latency is time per request; throughput is completed work per time period. In interviews, explain the concept, when it applies, and the trade-off it introduces. Use concrete examples from the provided material instead of definitions alone.
examples: A service may handle high throughput while one slow endpoint has bad latency.

questions.prompt: Match the reliability signal to what it tells you.
questions.explanation: Averages hide pain. Interview answers should separate per-request latency, total capacity, and tail latency.

concept_panel.title: Latency, Throughput, and Tail Latency
concept_panel.explanation: Latency is how long one operation takes. Throughput is how many operations complete per unit of time. Percentiles such as p95 and p99 reveal the slow tail that averages hide. Systems can have acceptable average latency while still hurting users at the tail.
key_takeaways: Latency measures time per request.
Throughput measures capacity over time.
p95/p99 expose slow user experiences hidden by averages.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can measure performance in user-visible terms.
concept_panel.practical_example: A checkout endpoint averaging 120 ms can still be bad if p99 is 4 seconds.

questions.prompt: A product catalog is read thousands of times and changes rarely. What is the first likely optimization?
questions.explanation: Caches are strongest when the same data is read repeatedly and can tolerate controlled staleness.

concept_panel.title: Caching
concept_panel.explanation: A cache stores previously computed or fetched data so repeated reads avoid expensive work. Caching improves latency and reduces load, but introduces staleness and invalidation problems. You should cache data that is read often, expensive to compute, and safe to serve slightly stale. Always explain cache hit, cache miss, TTL, and invalidation.
key_takeaways: Cache hits avoid database or service work.
Cache misses still need the source of truth.
Invalidation and staleness are the main trade-offs.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand performance trade-offs and stale-data risk.
concept_panel.practical_example: A product catalog can be cached in Redis with a TTL if updates are infrequent.

questions.prompt: A public API is being hammered by one client and starving others. What protects the service?
questions.explanation: Rate limits cap request volume per client or key so shared resources remain available.

concept_panel.title: Rate Limiting
concept_panel.explanation: Rate limiting caps how much traffic a client, user, or API key can send. It protects shared resources from abuse, accidental loops, and noisy neighbors. Rate limits should return clear errors and may include retry-after information. They are part of reliability and fairness, not only security.
key_takeaways: Rate limits protect shared capacity.
Limits are usually per client, user, token, or IP.
Clear retry behavior improves client reliability.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand API protection and fairness under load.
concept_panel.practical_example: Allow 100 requests per minute per API key and return 429 when exceeded.

questions.prompt: A failed downstream service causes every caller to retry instantly until the whole system slows down. What is the bug?
questions.explanation: Retries need limits, jitter, and exponential backoff. Instant retries can amplify the original outage.

concept_panel.title: Timeouts, Retries, and Backoff
concept_panel.explanation: Timeouts bound how long a caller waits for a dependency. A timeout leaves the outcome unknown: the downstream operation may still complete. Retries can help transient failures, but they need limits, jitter, and exponential backoff to avoid retry storms. The best design combines timeouts, idempotency, and observability.
key_takeaways: Timeout means unknown outcome, not guaranteed failure.
Retries need backoff and limits.
Unsafe operations need idempotency before retrying.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand reliability under partial failure.
concept_panel.practical_example: Retry a payment POST only with an idempotency key and a bounded retry policy.

questions.prompt: A dependency sometimes hangs forever. What should every outbound call include?
questions.explanation: Timeouts bound waiting and free resources. Without them, stuck dependencies can exhaust worker capacity.

questions.prompt: A payment provider is failing and repeated calls are wasting threads. Which pattern should temporarily stop calls?
questions.explanation: A circuit breaker stops sending traffic to a dependency that is already failing, then probes for recovery.

concept_panel.title: Circuit Breakers
concept_panel.explanation: A circuit breaker stops sending requests to a dependency that is repeatedly failing. Instead of tying up resources with calls likely to fail, the service fails fast or uses fallback behavior. After a cool-down period, it probes to see whether the dependency has recovered. This protects both the caller and the struggling dependency.
key_takeaways: Circuit breakers prevent repeated failing calls.
Fail-fast behavior protects resources.
Recovery usually uses limited probe requests.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand cascading failure prevention.
concept_panel.practical_example: If the payment provider returns errors for a sustained window, open the circuit and show a retry-later response.

questions.prompt: Checkout receives bursty order events, but processing can happen asynchronously. What smooths the spike?
questions.explanation: Queues buffer bursts and let workers process at a controlled pace, trading immediacy for resilience.

concept_panel.title: Queues and Backpressure
concept_panel.explanation: A queue decouples producers from workers. It smooths bursts by storing work until consumers can process it, which improves resilience but adds delay. Queues are useful when immediate completion is not required. The design must handle retries, duplicates, dead-letter queues, and visibility into lag.
key_takeaways: Queues smooth bursty writes.
Async processing trades immediacy for resilience.
Consumer lag and duplicate handling matter.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you understand async system design and backpressure.
concept_panel.practical_example: Send email jobs to a queue so signup responses do not wait for the email provider.

questions.prompt: Match observability data to its best use.
questions.explanation: Logs, metrics, and traces answer different production questions; strong debugging uses all three.

concept_panel.title: Logs, Metrics, and Traces
concept_panel.explanation: Observability gives evidence about production behavior. Logs explain specific events, metrics show trends and rates, and traces follow one request across services. Good incident answers use these signals to narrow the problem instead of guessing. Observability should be designed before the system is failing.
key_takeaways: Logs explain individual events.
Metrics reveal trends, rates, and percentiles.
Traces expose cross-service latency and failures.
concept_panel.interview_insight: Interviewers usually ask this concept to evaluate whether you can debug production systems with evidence.
concept_panel.practical_example: A slow checkout trace can show that inventory, not payments, dominates latency.

questions.prompt: Recommendations fail, but the product page can still load. What should the API do?
questions.explanation: Graceful degradation keeps the core user path working when optional features fail.

questions.prompt: An endpoint makes 15 downstream calls serially and p99 latency explodes. What should you examine first?
questions.explanation: Serial fan-out stacks latency and increases the chance that one slow dependency dominates the whole request.

coding_challenges.title: Performance and Reliability status classifier
coding_challenges.instructions: Implement classify_status_code(code: int) -> str. Return success for 200-299, redirect for 300-399, client_error for 400-499, server_error for 500-599, and unknown otherwise.
coding_challenges.explanation: The challenge reinforces deterministic branching, status-code categories, and local test execution.
